Metamaterials exhibit unique electromagnetic properties due to embedded structures.
Double negative (DNG) metamaterials have negative permittivity and permeability.
Radar cross section (RCS) measurements reveal frequency-dependent scattering angles.
RCS measurements are effective for characterizing bulk metamaterial samples.
CST Microwave Studio transient solver predicted resonant bands about 1 GHz below measurements.
CST Microwave Studio frequency solver resonant bands closely matched measurements but are computationally intensive.
Metamaterial operational bandwidth is limited by narrow resonant bands of embedded structures.
Adaptive metamaterial design incorporates MEMS variable capacitors in SRR gaps.
Applying voltage to MEMS capacitors changes effective capacitance and resonant frequency.
Resonant frequencies for a 4.0 scale adaptive metamaterial vary from 2.17 to 0.68 GHz.
Resonant frequencies for a 4.9 scale adaptive metamaterial vary from 1.93 to 0.608 GHz.
Reducing the gap in SRR elements facilitates MEMS capacitor fabrication with minimal impact on resonance.
Computational models of passive metamaterials agree well with experimental measurements.
Bistatic RCS measurement technique was developed and applied to metamaterial wedge samples.
MEMS capacitors enable dynamic tuning of metamaterial electromagnetic properties.
Split ring resonators (SRRs) are fundamental components in achieving negative permeability.
Frequency adaptability is key to overcoming metamaterial bandwidth limitations.
The thesis includes detailed computational and experimental studies validating adaptive metamaterial designs.
The research advances methods for characterizing electromagnetic field behavior in metamaterials.
Future research is recommended to enhance passive and adaptive metamaterial characterization and design.
